_comment: Book background and notes on the text for the study prompt (generate.request_values). Read by a person before any batch. Widely held views only; anything contested goes under disputes. textNotes apply to every verse from..to (KJV keys) and are the only manuscript facts the model may mention. Editing this file changes the prompt hash.

MAT.author: Anonymous; early church tradition names Matthew, the tax collector who became an apostle.
MAT.date: Probably between about AD 70 and 90; some date it before AD 70.
MAT.audience: Probably mostly Jewish followers of Jesus, perhaps in Syria; it often shows Jesus fulfilling Israel's Scriptures.
MAT.setting: Jesus's birth, his teaching and healing in Galilee, his journey to Jerusalem, his death and resurrection.
disputes: Whether the apostle Matthew wrote it as we have it is disputed.
How the first three Gospels relate is debated; most scholars think Matthew used Mark, others think Matthew came first.

MRK.author: Anonymous; early church tradition names John Mark and links his Gospel to Peter's preaching.
MRK.audience: Probably mostly non-Jewish believers; it explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words. Tradition places it in Rome.
MRK.setting: Jesus's ministry in Galilee, his journey to Jerusalem, and his last week, death and resurrection, told at a fast pace.
disputes: The author's identity and the link to Peter are disputed.
Where it was written (Rome, Syria or Galilee) is disputed.
Most scholars think Mark was the first Gospel written, but this is debated.
Whether the original ending is at 16:8 is disputed.

LUK.author: Anonymous; early church tradition names Luke, a doctor and companion of Paul. The same author wrote Acts.
LUK.date: Probably around AD 80 to 90; some date it to the early 60s.
LUK.audience: Written for Theophilus and, through him, probably for non-Jewish readers; it stresses God's welcome for outsiders, the poor and women.
LUK.setting: Jesus's birth, his ministry in Galilee, a long journey to Jerusalem, his death, resurrection and ascension.
disputes: Whether the author was Paul's companion Luke is disputed.
Which earlier sources Luke used is debated.

JHN.author: Anonymous; it is linked to "the disciple whom Jesus loved", whom tradition identifies as the apostle John.
JHN.date: Probably around AD 90 to 100; some date it earlier.
JHN.audience: Written so that readers may believe Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and have life. Tradition places it in Ephesus.
JHN.setting: Jesus's signs and long conversations, several visits to Jerusalem at the festivals, his last night with his disciples, his death and resurrection.
disputes: Who the beloved disciple was, and whether he wrote the book himself, is disputed.
Whether the book grew in stages is debated.
How John relates to the other three Gospels is debated.

PSA.author: Many poets. Headings attribute many psalms to David and others to Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses and others; many have no heading.
PSA.date: Written over several centuries, from the time of the kings to after the exile; the collection was probably completed after the exile.
PSA.audience: Israel at worship, in the temple and in personal prayer; the church has prayed them ever since.
PSA.setting: Praise, thanksgiving, lament, confession, trust, royal and wisdom poems, gathered into five books.
disputes: Whether the headings are original or added later is disputed.
The dates of most individual psalms are disputed.
Psalm numbering differs in Bibles based on the Greek translation, usually by one.
